title: Clean Code
subtitle: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship

oneLine.text: Code is read far more than it is written, so write it for the next reader: small, named, tested, honest.

pullQuote.text: Clean code is a team agreement, not a personal virtue. Put the agreement in CI and stop arguing about it in review.

items.name: Meaningful names
items.gist: Names should reveal intent, so a reader never has to decode them.

items.name: Small functions
items.gist: A function should do one thing, at one level of abstraction, with few arguments.

items.name: Comments
items.gist: Prefer code that explains itself; a comment often marks a failure to express intent in code.

items.name: Formatting
items.gist: Consistent layout is communication; a team should agree on one style and follow it.

items.name: Error handling
items.gist: Use exceptions rather than error codes, and don’t return or pass null.

items.name: Unit tests
items.gist: Tests deserve the same care as production code: fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating, timely.

items.name: Classes
items.gist: Keep classes small, with a single reason to change.

items.name: The Boy Scout Rule
items.gist: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it, every time.

sections.body: Clean Code is the book that gave a generation of engineers, me included, a shared language for code quality. I keep it on the shelf less as a rulebook and more as a reminder that readable code is a kindness to the next person, and now to the next agent, that has to change it.

Martin argues that code is read far more often than it is written, so the main cost of software is understanding and changing it. Clean code is code a reader can follow without effort: well-named, small, tested and free of surprises. Writing it is a discipline of continuous small improvements rather than occasional big rewrites.

- I treat readability as a team standard, not a matter of taste: we agree on conventions once and let linters and formatters enforce them, so review time goes to design, not style.
- “CI lands the work” is the rule my agent fleet runs under, and clean code is what makes that safe: small, well-tested changes are the only kind a required check can judge.
- I ask for the Boy Scout Rule in every change: leave the touched code a little better, and keep the cleanup in the same small PR.
- When an agent writes code, I hold it to the same bar as a person. Names, small functions and tests are what let a reviewer, human or AI, actually review it.

- Could a new engineer explain what this module does after ten minutes of reading?
- Which of our naming or style arguments could a tool settle for us?
- When did we last leave code cleaner than we found it, in a change that wasn’t a dedicated refactor?
- Are our tests clear enough to read as documentation?
- Where are we tolerating a function nobody wants to touch, and why?

The core claim is right and has aged well: code is read far more than it is written, and the cost of a codebase is the cost of understanding it. Small, well-named units and tests you can trust are still the foundation of a team that moves fast safely.

The examples are dated and Java-centric, and some rules are contested in practice. Very small functions can scatter logic across files and make code harder to follow, not easier, and a blanket suspicion of comments undersells comments that explain why. Followed as dogma, the book produces cleverness in the name of cleanliness; it works best as a set of defaults a team adapts and agrees on.

- Write for the reader; that reader is now often an agent too.
- Agree on standards once, then automate them.
- Small, safe improvements beat big rewrites.
- Treat test code as production code.
- Rules are defaults, not dogma.
Read it with **Extreme Programming Explained**: Clean Code is the craft inside the practices; XP is the system that makes the craft routine.
Skip it if you want current, language-specific guidance; it’s a 2008 book with Java examples. It misleads teams that turn its heuristics into hard rules and fight about function length in review.

ideas.title: Code is read more than written
ideas.summary: Most of the time spent on code goes into reading and understanding it, so optimizing for the reader pays off.
ideas.caveat: How much this matters depends on the code’s lifespan; throwaway scripts don’t need the same care.
ideas.example: A service that many teams touch gets cheaper to change every time someone improves its names.

ideas.title: Functions should do one thing
ideas.summary: Small functions at a single level of abstraction are easier to name, test and understand.
ideas.caveat: Pushed too far, tiny functions fragment logic and make flow harder to follow.

ideas.title: Comments are often a smell
ideas.summary: Prefer expressing intent in code; comments drift out of date and can hide unclear code.
ideas.caveat: Comments that explain why, or record a decision, remain valuable and are often missing.

ideas.title: Tests are first-class code
ideas.summary: Tests should be clean, fast and independent, because a suite nobody trusts gets ignored.
ideas.caveat: Test style is also contested; the book’s preferences aren’t the only workable approach.
ideas.example: A team with readable tests uses them as documentation for how the system is meant to behave.

ideas.title: Leave it cleaner than you found it
ideas.summary: Continuous small improvements keep a codebase healthy without big rewrites.
ideas.caveat: Opportunistic cleanup can bloat changes; keep it small and reviewable.
